title: Interfaces vs Type Aliases
summary: **Interfaces** and **type aliases** both name shapes, and they overlap heavily — but interfaces can be *merged* and *extended* for object/class contracts, while type aliases can express *unions, intersections, tuples, and mapped/derived types* that interfaces cannot.

subtopics.title: What each can express
subtopics.explanation: Both can name an object shape and both can be generic. But only a type alias can name a union, a tuple, a primitive alias, or a mapped/conditional type. Only an interface can be reopened (declaration merging). For plain object shapes they're nearly interchangeable.
subtopics.example:
type ID = string | number; // alias only
interface User { id: ID; }

subtopics.title: Declaration merging (interface only)
subtopics.explanation: Declaring an interface name twice merges the members; declaring a type alias twice is a duplicate-identifier error. Merging is what makes interfaces the right choice for types meant to be augmented — globals, library types, or public API surfaces.
subtopics.example:
interface W { a: number }
interface W { b: number } // merges to { a; b }

subtopics.title: extends vs intersection
subtopics.explanation: Interfaces compose with extends; type aliases compose with the & intersection operator. extends actively checks that the child is compatible with the parent and reports conflicts as errors; an intersection silently combines members and can produce never for incompatible conflicts.
subtopics.example:
interface B extends A {}
type B = A & { extra: string };

subtopics.title: Unions, tuples, and mapped types
subtopics.explanation: These are the things only a type alias can do. Discriminated unions, fixed-length tuples, key remapping, conditional types, and template-literal types are all expressed with type. If your shape isn't a plain object, you almost certainly need a type alias.
subtopics.example: type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string };

subtopics.title: Performance and error messages
subtopics.explanation: The compiler caches interfaces by name and can compare them efficiently, while large intersection-heavy aliases may be slower to check. Errors involving named interfaces often read more cleanly ('Type X is not assignable to User') than fully-expanded intersection aliases.
subtopics.example:
// interface error: '... not assignable to User'
// alias error: may expand the whole intersection

subtopics.title: Generics with both
subtopics.explanation: Interfaces and type aliases can both take type parameters, so generic object shapes can use either. The deciding factors are merging/extension (favor interface) versus union/mapped/derived needs (require type), not generics themselves.
subtopics.example:
interface Box<T> { value: T }
type Box2<T> = { value: T };

subtopics.title: Team conventions
subtopics.explanation: Many teams adopt a simple rule: use interface for object and class shapes that may be extended or implemented, and type for unions, tuples, and derived types. Consistency matters more than the specific choice, since the two are interchangeable for most object shapes.
subtopics.example: // convention: interface for props, type for unions

foundations.overview: Interfaces and type aliases are TypeScript's two ways to name a type, and for ordinary object shapes they're almost interchangeable. The differences matter at the edges: interfaces support declaration merging and a checked extends relationship, making them ideal for extensible contracts and class implementation; type aliases can name anything — unions, intersections, tuples, primitives, and mapped/conditional types — making them essential for non-object shapes. Knowing which capability each has lets you pick the right tool instead of guessing.
foundations.formalDefinition: An interface is a named, open (mergeable) structural object type that supports extends and implements. A type alias is a name bound to any type expression — object, union, intersection, tuple, primitive, function, mapped, or conditional — and is closed (cannot be redeclared or merged).
foundations.whyItMatters: Choosing wrongly leads to friction: trying to express a union as an interface is impossible, and relying on declaration merging with a type alias fails. Picking the capable construct keeps types expressible, error messages clean, and public APIs extensible. It's also a perennial interview question precisely because it tests depth of TypeScript knowledge.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of interface as an extensible blueprint for objects — it can be reopened and inherited. Think of type as a label you can stick on absolutely any type expression, including ones interfaces can't describe. When the shape is a plain extensible object, either works; when it's a union or derived type, only the label works.
foundations.browserPerspective: Both are purely compile-time constructs and are fully erased — the emitted JavaScript is identical whether you used an interface or a type alias. The choice affects only the developer experience and the compiler, never the runtime.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Interfaces are common for React props, public library types, and class contracts (implements). Type aliases dominate for discriminated unions (Result/Action), tuple return types, function signatures, and utility-type compositions like Partial<T> & { id: string }.
foundations.businessImpact: Using mergeable interfaces for public API types lets consumers augment them without forking, while expressive type aliases model domain states (success/error variants) precisely, reducing invalid-state bugs that reach customers.
foundations.engineeringImpact: A consistent interface-vs-type convention removes a recurring micro-decision from code review and keeps the codebase predictable, while choosing the capable construct avoids painful rewrites when a shape later needs a union or merging.
foundations.performanceImpact: Both are erased, so there's no runtime cost. At compile time, interfaces are cached by name and compared efficiently, whereas large, deeply nested intersection aliases can slow the type-checker and produce more verbose errors.
commonUseCases: Interface for React props and extensible object contracts
Type alias for discriminated unions (Result, Action)
Type alias for tuples, function types, and mapped/derived types
Interface for public library types meant to be augmented

commonMisconceptions.myth: Interfaces and types are completely interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They overlap for object shapes, but only types express unions/tuples/mapped types and only interfaces support declaration merging. The capabilities differ at the edges.
They can be composed with intersections (A & B) and even extended by interfaces; they just can't be reopened and merged the way interfaces can.

visualExplorer.title: Picking interface or type alias
visualExplorer.caption: Walk a decision path from the shape you need to the right construct, noting the capability that decides it.

config.intro: Decide between interface and type alias based on what your shape needs to do.

steps.name: Is it a plain object shape?
steps.detail: If you're naming an object's properties/methods, both work — fall through to the next questions.

steps.name: Does it need a union or tuple?
steps.detail: Unions (A | B), tuples, and primitive aliases require a type alias — interfaces can't express them.

steps.name: Is it mapped or conditional?
steps.detail: Mapped types, key remapping, conditional and template-literal types only exist as type aliases.

steps.name: Will it be augmented or merged?
steps.detail: Public/library/global types that consumers should extend favor interfaces, thanks to declaration merging.

steps.name: Is a class implementing it?
steps.detail: implements works most naturally with an interface contract.

steps.name: Otherwise, follow convention
steps.detail: For interchangeable object shapes, pick whatever your team standardizes on — consistency beats the toss-up.

interactiveExamples.title: The interchangeable case
interactiveExamples.explanation: For a plain object shape, an interface and a type alias produce the same checked result.

interactiveExamples.title: Where only type works
interactiveExamples.explanation: Unions and discriminated unions can't be expressed as interfaces — this is the clear case for a type alias.

interactiveExamples.title: Where only interface merges
interactiveExamples.explanation: Reopening an interface merges members; doing the same with a type alias is a duplicate-identifier error.

codeLab.title: Model a payment state correctly
codeLab.instructions: A payment is either pending, succeeded (with a transactionId), or failed (with a reason). Choose the right construct to model this as a discriminated union named Payment, then write summarize(p: Payment) returning a description string.
codeLab.expectedOutput: pending then ok tx_1 then failed declined
hints: A union of object shapes can only be named with a type alias, not an interface.
Use a shared 'status' discriminant so each branch narrows to the right fields.

debuggingLab.title: Trying to express a union as an interface
debuggingLab.symptom: A developer wants Status to be 'on' or 'off' but reaches for an interface, then can't make the union work and falls back to a loose string.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: An interface field can only hold a single type, so the literal union 'on' | 'off' was widened to string. That lets invalid values like 'of' through and disables exhaustiveness, so the typo silently produces wrong behavior.
commonMistakes: Reaching for an interface when the shape is fundamentally a union.
Widening to string instead of using a literal union to constrain values.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Use a type alias to model the literal union so invalid values are compile errors.

theory.question: What's the difference between an interface and a type alias?
theory.directAnswer: Both name types and overlap for object shapes, but each has unique abilities. Only an interface supports declaration merging (reopening to add members) and the checked extends/implements relationship, making it ideal for extensible object and class contracts. Only a type alias can name unions, intersections, tuples, primitives, and mapped or conditional types. The rule of thumb: interface for extensible object shapes, type for anything that isn't a plain object — and pick by team convention when they're interchangeable.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two constructs for naming types: interface (open, object-focused) and type alias (closed, any type expression).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Interfaces model extensible structural contracts; type aliases give a name to arbitrary type expressions the compiler can't otherwise reference.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interfaces merge by name and compose via extends; type aliases are bound once and compose via & and | operators. Both are erased at compile time.

theory.whyImportant: It tests whether a candidate understands TypeScript's type system beyond surface syntax and can choose the right tool for each shape.
theory.realWorldExample: Component props are typically an interface (extensible), while a Redux action is a discriminated union type alias.

nestedTopics.title: Declaration merging
nestedTopics.explanation: Interfaces reopen and merge; type aliases can't be redeclared.

nestedTopics.title: Union/mapped types
nestedTopics.explanation: Only type aliases can express unions, tuples, and mapped types.

nestedTopics.title: extends vs &
nestedTopics.explanation: Interfaces use extends (checked); aliases use intersection (silent combine).

followUps.question: Can an interface extend a type alias?
followUps.answer: Yes, as long as the alias resolves to an object type (or intersection of object types). It can't extend a union alias, since interfaces can't represent unions.

followUps.question: Is one faster than the other?
followUps.answer: For object shapes, interfaces are cached by name and tend to type-check efficiently with cleaner errors; large intersection-heavy aliases can be slower and produce more verbose messages.

theory.question: When should you prefer a type alias over an interface, and vice versa?
theory.directAnswer: Prefer a type alias whenever the shape isn't a plain object — unions, tuples, primitive aliases, function types, and mapped or conditional types all require one. Prefer an interface for object and class contracts that may be extended (extends), implemented by classes (implements), or augmented by consumers (declaration merging), such as public library types and React props. When both work, follow your team's convention for consistency.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A capability-driven decision between the two naming constructs.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because each construct can express things the other cannot, the shape's requirements dictate the choice.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Check whether you need a union/mapped/derived type (type) or merging/extension/implementation of an object contract (interface); default to convention otherwise.

theory.whyImportant: Picking the capable construct prevents impossible-to-express types and avoids rewrites when a shape later grows new requirements.
theory.realWorldExample: A public design-system Theme type is often an interface so apps can merge in custom tokens; a Result<T> success/error type must be a union alias.

nestedTopics.title: Augmentation needs
nestedTopics.explanation: If consumers should extend the type, merging makes interface the right call.

nestedTopics.title: Derived types
nestedTopics.explanation: Partial<T>, Pick<T,K>, and key remapping live as type aliases.

followUps.question: What if a type starts as an object but later needs a union?
followUps.answer: If there's any chance it becomes a union, a type alias is safer, since you'd otherwise have to migrate from interface to type and update extends/implements usages.

scenario.question: You're publishing a shared types package for several apps. Some shapes are extensible config objects, others are success/error result variants. How do you decide interface vs type for each?
scenario.directAnswer: Model the extensible config objects as interfaces so downstream apps can augment them via declaration merging (e.g., adding custom config fields) and extend them with extends. Model the result variants as type aliases, since success/error states are a discriminated union that interfaces can't express. Document the convention in the package so consumers know which types are meant to be augmented, and keep derived types (Partial, Pick) as type aliases too.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Applying the capability rule across a public API surface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Library consumers benefit from augmentable interfaces, while domain states need precise unions.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Interfaces stay open for merging/extension; union and derived shapes use type aliases that the compiler can fully describe.

scenario.whyImportant: Public type design is hard to change later; choosing the right construct upfront avoids breaking consumers.

nestedTopics.title: Module augmentation
nestedTopics.explanation: Consumers merge into your interfaces to add fields without forking the package.

nestedTopics.title: Discriminated unions
nestedTopics.explanation: Result/Status variants must be type aliases with a shared discriminant.

followUps.question: Why not make everything a type alias for consistency?
followUps.answer: Then consumers lose declaration merging, so they can't cleanly augment your config types without forking — a real downside for a shared package.

coding.question: Given a base interface Entity { id: string }, show two ways to add a createdAt field: extending with an interface and composing with a type intersection. Then explain a behavioral difference.
coding.thoughtProcess: First I'll define the base Entity interface. Then I'll build a Timestamped version two ways: an interface using extends, and a type alias using the & intersection. Both yield { id; createdAt }. The behavioral difference to highlight: the interface version can be reopened/merged and gives checked extends errors, while the intersection silently combines and can collapse conflicting members to never. I'll demonstrate both compile to the same usable shape.
coding.lineByLine: Entity is the shared base. TimestampedI extends Entity, inheriting id and adding createdAt with a checked relationship. TimestampedT intersects Entity with a new member object to the same effect. Both constants type-check identically. The comment notes the key difference: interfaces support merging and report extends conflicts, whereas intersections silently combine and reduce incompatible members to never.
coding.timeComplexity: N/A — these are compile-time type constructs.

alternativeApproaches.title: Generic mixin via type
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A reusable type alias can add timestamps to any entity generically.
alternativeApproaches.code:
type WithTimestamp<T> = T & { createdAt: number };
// type X = WithTimestamp<Entity>;

followUps.question: When does an intersection produce never?
followUps.answer: When two members share a key with incompatible types (e.g., id: string in one and id: number in the other), the intersection of those types is never, making the property unusable — extends would instead surface it as an error.

productionDeepDive.architecture: In a real codebase the split tends to be: interfaces for object/class contracts (props, DTOs, service interfaces, public/augmentable library types) and type aliases for unions, tuples, function types, and derived/utility compositions. Public packages lean on interfaces so consumers can augment via declaration merging, while internal domain states use precise discriminated unions.
productionDeepDive.performance: Both are erased, so runtime is unaffected. At compile time, interfaces are referenced by a stable name and compared efficiently; heavy use of large, nested intersection type aliases can increase type-checking time and inflate error output, so prefer interfaces or simpler compositions for hot, widely-used shapes.
productionDeepDive.security: Neither construct validates data at runtime, so the choice has no direct security implication — untrusted input must still be validated regardless. The relevant discipline is the same as with any TypeScript type: don't assume external data matches the declared shape.
productionDeepDive.scaling: A documented convention (interface for extensible objects, type for unions/derived) removes a recurring decision and keeps a growing codebase consistent. Using interfaces for public types preserves consumers' ability to augment them as the system scales across teams.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Consistency is the main lever: pick a rule, encode it (e.g., via lint rules like consistent-type-definitions), and follow it. Favor interface extends for object inheritance because conflicts are reported, and reserve intersections for genuine compositions where silent combination is acceptable.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI enforces both kinds of contracts. Cleaner interface error messages make build failures faster to diagnose than deeply expanded intersection-alias errors, which is a small but real maintainability win at scale.

caseStudies.problem: Consumers needed to augment library types, and domain states needed precise variants.
caseStudies.solution: Exposed augmentable shapes as interfaces (merging-friendly) and modeled variant states as discriminated union type aliases.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Two constructs to reason about vs. each type using its most capable form.
caseStudies.lessons: Interfaces and types are complementary; choosing by capability — merging/extension vs. unions/derived — yields the most ergonomic and future-proof API.

projectBuilder.summary: Type the expense tracker's domain by deliberately choosing interfaces for extensible shapes and type aliases for state unions.
requirements: An extensible Expense interface (open for augmentation)
A LoadState discriminated union as a type alias
A derived type (e.g., DraftExpense) via a utility type alias
projectBuilder.architecture: Expense is an interface so feature modules can merge in extra fields. The async UI state is a type alias LoadState = { status: 'idle' } | { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'error'; message: string } | { status: 'ready'; data: Expense[] }. A DraftExpense = Omit<Expense, 'id'> type alias derives the create form's shape.

steps.title: Expense interface
steps.instructions: Define Expense as an interface so it can be augmented later.
steps.checkpoint: A feature module can merge an extra field via declaration merging.

steps.title: LoadState union
steps.instructions: Model the four async states as a discriminated union type alias.
steps.checkpoint: Each status narrows to exactly the fields it carries.

steps.title: Derived DraftExpense
steps.instructions: Use type DraftExpense = Omit<Expense, 'id'> for the create form.
steps.checkpoint: DraftExpense automatically tracks Expense changes minus id.

enhancements: Add WithTimestamp<T> = T & { createdAt: number } and apply it to Expense
Enforce the convention with the consistent-type-definitions lint rule
interviewQuestions: Why is Expense an interface but LoadState a type alias?
How does deriving DraftExpense from Expense keep them in sync?

keyTakeaways: Interfaces and type aliases overlap for object shapes but differ at the edges — choose by capability.
Only interfaces support declaration merging and the checked extends/implements relationship.
Only type aliases can name unions, intersections, tuples, primitives, and mapped/conditional types.
extends reports conflicts; intersections silently combine and can collapse incompatible members to never.
Rule of thumb: interface for extensible object/class contracts, type for unions and derived types — and stay consistent.
